solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Last month, university student overturned skip

parts.note: L is a learner, from the L-plate a learner driver displays

indicators.note: in a down clue, overturned means the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: to skip something is to omit it

explanation.surface: A student at university has tipped over a rubbish skip some time last month.
explanation.walkthrough: A British skip is a large open rubbish container, which is the picture the surface paints; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimo is a dated commercial term in letters meaning of the previous calendar month.

clue.text: Regret very much in hearing influential thinker

indicators.note: in hearing says the phrase is to be judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: to regret is to rue, and very much is so, giving rue so

explanation.surface: Someone at a hearing deeply regrets something an influential philosopher said.
explanation.walkthrough: RUE SO, said out loud, sounds like the name of the philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was an eighteenth-century philosopher whose ideas shaped the French Revolution.

clue.text: One concluding art with no merit should be scrapped

indicators.note: scrapping the arrangement of these letters means breaking them up and remaking them

explanation.surface: A critic says art without merit ought to be thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Should be scrapped' shuffles ART and NO MERIT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminator is anything that brings something to an end, as one concluding it.

clue.text: See impact that's explosive in continuum

indicators.note: an explosion blows these letters apart so they land in a new order

explanation.surface: Witness an explosive collision somewhere in the continuum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's explosive' rearranges SEE IMPACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics treats space and time as one four-dimensional continuum.

clue.text: Tramp lodged in waste-pipe

indicators.note: lodged in says the letters sit inside the written word that follows

explanation.surface: A vagrant has got himself stuck inside a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a homeless person; it is the verb, to walk heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to tread heavily, so it can stand for the verb step.

clue.text: Iron Lady displays top fashion

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
Dora is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher, the Iron Lady, shows off the latest high fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Lady' suggests Margaret Thatcher, but the two words work separately: a chemical symbol and a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A top is slang for a hat, and this felt hat with a creased crown is a stylish one.

clue.text: Swiss town stables unbelievable horse

indicators.note: stables, as a verb, means houses something within it

parts.note: Sion is a town in the Swiss canton of Valais
a tall story is an unbelievable one

explanation.surface: A Swiss town keeps an amazing horse in its stables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stables' looks like a noun, but it is the verb: SION holds TALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse.

clue.text: She might be found in India, applied to feeding minor

indicators.note: feeding means going into, as food goes into a mouth

parts.note: minor means less, as in lesser
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet
something applied to a surface is on it

explanation.surface: A careful note on where an animal lives and how a medicine is given to a child.
explanation.walkthrough: Asiatic lions survive in India's Gir Forest, so the female could be found there; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The female lion is a she among big cats, so 'she' plus a hint of habitat points to her.

clue.text: Almost broke cover

indicators.note: almost means the word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: skint is British slang for having no money, broke

explanation.surface: Someone nearly smashed a lid or casing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last letter of SKINT. SKINT is everyday British slang for penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin is the outer covering of a body or fruit, so a cover in a noun sense.

clue.text: Job description?

parts.note: the biblical Job is proverbial for long-suffering endurance, so the word describing him is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' at the start hides its capital: it is the biblical figure, not employment, and 'the patience of Job' is a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase the patience of Job makes this adjective the classic description of the biblical sufferer.

clue.text: I'm in as Con, corrupt, having no cause for alarm?

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or perverted, so the letters are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A prisoner admits he is inside as a convict, being crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' shuffles I'M IN AS CON. The definition is playful: someone who never sleeps needs no alarm clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who cannot sleep has no reason to set an alarm clock to wake up.

clue.text: Where one sees stem and large stalk

parts.note: the stem is the front timber of a ship, found at the bow
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A gardener describes a plant with a big stem and stalk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stem' and 'stalk' look like botany; the stem is the bow timber of a ship and stalk is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stalk prey is to move about stealthily hunting, the same as to roam about on the hunt.

clue.text: Round container Popeye ultimately dropped in sea

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: dropped in means placed inside the container

parts.note: a can is a container

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Popeye drops a round tin of spinach into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popeye ultimately' gives E, which goes inside CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean is one of the great bodies of salt water, a sea in a broad sense.

clue.text: Outside of Tours, a friend there gives wave

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters

parts.note: Tours is in France, so there a friend is un ami in French

explanation.surface: Outside the French city of Tours, a friend waves hello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside of' takes TS from Tours, and 'there' sends us to French.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea wave set off by an earthquake.

clue.text: Dread, thus considered, that can't be handled?

definitions.text: Dread, thus considered, that can't be handled?

parts.words: Dread, thus considered, that can't be handled?
parts.note: a dread too great to name is described this way, and a handle is slang for a name, so what cannot be handled cannot be named

explanation.walkthrough: A handle is slang for a name, so something that can't be handled is something that can't be named; nameless dread is a set phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Something too terrible or awful to put into words cannot be given a name.

clue.text: Outline from an unintelligent judge

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, the same as a
dumb is informal for stupid
to rate something is to judge its worth

explanation.surface: A sketch of a stupid magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a noun but here it is the verb, to assess.
explanation.definitionFit: To adumbrate is to sketch or indicate faintly, giving a rough outline.

clue.text: Before working hours, find time to make time?

indicators.note: to make here means to build a new arrangement out of the letters

parts.note: a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Before your shift starts, carve out some time for yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To make' is the anagram signal; 'Before' only links, and 'working' supplies two letters to the pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Relativity treats time as a further coordinate after the three of space.

clue.text: One tells stories, but fails to move

indicators.note: letters that move are shifted out of their places into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A narrator has a gift for tales but cannot get anyone stirred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To move' shuffles BUT FAILS.
explanation.definitionFit: A fabulist is a teller of fables, or more broadly of tall tales and lies.

clue.text: Unseemly and annoying child catcher?

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous, troublesome child
a roper catches cattle with a lasso

explanation.surface: A child catcher, like the villain who snatches children, is both indecent and irritating.
explanation.definitionFit: Improper conduct is unbecoming, not in keeping with good manners.

clue.text: Spot youngster spinning cloth

indicators.note: spinning means the pair of words is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a spot is a mark
a cub is a young animal, or a junior Scout

explanation.surface: Someone notices a child twirling a piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinning' turns MARKCUB round. 'Spinning' and 'cloth' suggest weaving; the spinning here is the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckram is a stiff cotton or linen fabric used in bookbinding and tailoring.

clue.text: Novelist showing briefly conflicting political positions

indicators.note: briefly means each word is cut short to its opening letters

parts.note: conservative and radical are opposing political stances

explanation.surface: An author is said to show clashing political views in brief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' shortens both CONSERVATIVE and RADICAL to their first three letters, leaving CON and RAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Conrad, author of Heart of Darkness, is a famous writer of fiction.

clue.text: Doctor straddling old exercise bike

indicators.note: straddling means sitting astride, with one letter on each side of the rest

parts.note: MD is a Doctor of Medicine
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: A doctor sits astride an old exercise bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straddling' puts O and PE between M and D.
explanation.definitionFit: A moped is a low-powered motorbike that can also be pedalled.

clue.text: Proper woman retiring as governess

parts.note: due means proper or fitting, as in due care

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so in a down clue the name reads upwards

parts.note: Ann is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A prim, shy lady works as a governess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proper' and 'retiring' look like character words for the governess; 'retiring' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A duenna is an older woman acting as chaperone and governess to girls in a Spanish family.

clue.text: Back by midnight? That's very curious!

parts.note: back in time means ago
the middle letter of the word night is G

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you'll be home by midnight, and wonders why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midnight' looks like the hour; it is the middle of the word night.
explanation.definitionFit: Being agog is being eagerly curious and excited to know more.

clue.text: Having shortened text, depart peculiar vocabulary

indicators.note: shortened means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a line is a piece of text, as in a line of verse
to go is to depart

explanation.surface: Someone sends an abbreviated text message and leaves, using odd words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortened' cuts LINE to LIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is jargon or language peculiar to a particular group.

clue.text: Try to quit search on Net producing lustful gaze

indicators.note: to quit means to leave, so this pair of letters departs from the longer word

parts.note: Google is the best-known internet search engine
a go is an attempt or try

explanation.surface: Giving up on an internet search ends in a leer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To quit' removes GO from GOOGLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogle is a leering, amorous stare, a look of desire.

clue.text: Process that confuses millions invested in capital part

indicators.note: invested in means put inside, as money is put into a business

parts.note: Riga is the capital of Latvia
M is the abbreviation for million
a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: A confusing procedure in which millions are poured into a part of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests money beside 'millions' and 'invested'; it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a long, complicated procedure that bewilders those caught in it.

clue.text: Call informers about potential lead

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the two words read backwards

parts.note: tel is short for telephone, a call
rats are informers

explanation.surface: A detective phones informers about a promising clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' turns TELRATS round. 'Potential lead' looks like a clue for police; it is a would-be leading actress.
explanation.definitionFit: A starlet is a young actress who may become a star in a leading role.

clue.text: Sound from kitchen aboard ship

indicators.note: sound from says the answer is how the phrase is pronounced

parts.note: a galley is a ship's kitchen, and aboard means on

explanation.surface: Noise comes from the kitchen on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: GALLEY ON, said out loud, gives the old sailing ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon was a large square-rigged sailing vessel of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
